The core insight is that introspective accounts do not reflect genuine phenomenological access but instead constitute a form of behavioral adjustment within structured contexts. This implies a dualism between naturalistic perception and laboratory-derived description. The 'running-back-and-forth' suggests iterative feedback mechanisms, while 'momentary sign-objects' indicate non-localized, unstable referents. These constructs imply that introspection operates under a distinct regime from ordinary cognition, where sensory data becomes abstracted into discrete, artifact-laden representations. The failure mode occurs when such abstraction detaches from ecological validity, leading to misalignment between reported mental states and actual behavioral outputs. Thus, the epistemological structure supports a Bayesian framework where introspective reports serve as noisy observations in a probabilistic model of cognition.
